title: Sleep under an insecticide-treated net every night
text: Sleeping under an insecticide-treated net (ITN) every night is the best-proven way to prevent malaria. In trials, treated nets cut child deaths by about 17%, severe malaria by 44%, and uncomplicated falciparum malaria episodes by almost half compared with no nets. Everyone in the house should use one, all year, including children and pregnant women. Treated nets still worked better than untreated nets, so they remain effective despite growing insecticide resistance.

title: Use the net correctly: tuck it in and repair holes
text: A net only protects when it is used correctly. Tuck the bottom edges under the mattress, check the net regularly for holes and sew them up. Nets work best when more than 80% of people in the community sleep under them. Because treated nets also kill mosquitoes that land on them, high community use protects neighbours as well as the family.

title: Anopheles bite from dusk to dawn, often early in the evening
text: Malaria mosquitoes (Anopheles) bite mainly between dusk and dawn, but local species differ. In Jayapura, Papua, Anopheles farauti was found biting early in the evening and indoors, and elsewhere this species shifted to biting outdoors in the early evening. The riskiest time is often the evening before going to bed: sitting outside, fishing or working at night. Long sleeves, trousers and repellent help cover this gap that nets leave.

title: Skin repellents: an evening and outdoor supplement to nets
text: Registered skin repellents such as DEET, picaridin (icaridin), IR3535 and oil of lemon eucalyptus (PMD) repel Anopheles mosquitoes well. Reviews found they may slightly reduce malaria infection, with the clearest benefit where people have no nets, and little or no extra benefit where nets are already used. Use them on exposed skin in the evening and outdoors, following the label, as a supplement to a net and never as a substitute. Side effects were rare.

title: Indoor spatial emanators, in addition to nets
text: In August 2025 WHO made a conditional recommendation for indoor spatial emanators, devices that release a repellent into the room, used in addition to insecticide-treated nets. It is the first new class of vector control product in more than 40 years. WHO advises using prequalified products only. Ordinary coils and plug-in devices are not the same as the prequalified products that were tested, and none of these replaces sleeping under a net.

source: Am J Trop Med Hyg (Syafruddin et al. 2020, Sumba trial)
title: Spatial repellents help most where transmission is intense
text: A cluster-randomized trial of transfluthrin spatial repellents in Sumba, East Nusa Tenggara, found a 28-31% protective effect across all villages, which was not statistically significant. In the moderate- to high-risk villages, protection rose to a significant 60%. In plain terms, spatial repellents add the most protection where malaria transmission is intense, and they are used on top of nets.

title: Screen windows, vents and eaves
text: Screening windows, doors and eaves probably reduces malaria infection: in trials, parasite prevalence fell by about a third and moderate-to-severe anaemia also fell. WHO conditionally recommends house screening. In a typical Indonesian house, fitting wire mesh (kawat kasa) to windows and air vents, closing gaps under the roof and repairing holes are cheap, practical steps that keep mosquitoes out at night.

source: Cochrane (Choi, Pryce & Garner 2019; Pryce et al. 2022)
title: Accept indoor residual spraying when the health programme offers it
text: Indoor residual spraying (IRS) means the health programme sprays a long-lasting insecticide on the inside walls of houses. Adding IRS with non-pyrethroid insecticides to nets was linked to less malaria, while pyrethroid IRS added no detectable benefit. IRS is a programme decision, not a do-it-yourself task: accept it when the puskesmas or health office offers it. It works best against mosquitoes that rest indoors, so it may help less where local vectors bite and rest outdoors.

source: Anopheles sundaicus complex in Indonesia (PMC 2020); Anopheles biodiversity review (2024)
title: Where malaria mosquitoes breed
text: Anopheles larvae prefer clean, often sunlit ground water: swamps, rice fields, ponds, stream edges, hoof prints and pools left after floods. Along Indonesia's coasts, Anopheles sundaicus breeds in sunlit brackish lagoons, often with floating algae mats. This differs from the dengue mosquito, Aedes aegypti, which breeds in clean water inside containers, so cleaning containers alone will not reach most malaria mosquito habitats.

source: WHO Guidelines for malaria (2025); Cochrane (Choi, Majambere & Wilson 2019)
title: Drain or fill standing water where breeding sites are few and findable
text: Removing breeding sites and larviciding help mainly where aquatic habitats are few, fixed and findable, such as a village edge with a few ponds or the dry season when water shrinks to a few pools. They did not help across kilometres of marsh. WHO says larviciding supplements nets or indoor spraying and should not be seen as a substitute. After floods, fill or drain new pools near houses early, because larvae develop in about 1 to 2 weeks, and ask the puskesmas about the biological larvicide Bti for permanent lagoons and fishponds.

source: PLOS Global Public Health (malaria early warning scoping review, 2025); Kemenkes technical guidance (2022)
title: Step up protection at the start of the rains and after floods
text: Malaria transmission in Indonesia is usually highest in the rainy season. Rain and heat act with a delay: cases often peak weeks to about two months after heavy rainfall, because mosquitoes need time to breed and infections take time to show. A practical rule is to step up net use, screening and testing at the start of the rains and during the 1 to 2 months after heavy rain or floods.

title: Get a malaria blood test the same day anyone has a fever
text: Anyone with a fever in a malaria area, or in the weeks after visiting one, should go to a health worker at the puskesmas or clinic for a malaria blood test the same day. Malaria often starts with fever, chills, headache and body aches and can look like flu or dengue, so it cannot be told apart by symptoms alone. Symptoms can appear one to several weeks after a bite. A prompt test and a completed course of treatment from a health worker prevent severe illness and stop further spread.

title: Before travelling to a high-risk area, see a doctor
text: Before visiting Papua or another high-risk malaria area, see a doctor one to two weeks before the trip to discuss how to prevent malaria; the right choice depends on the person and on the area. No prevention method is 100% effective, so keep sleeping under a net and using repellent during the trip. Anyone who gets a fever during or after the trip should be tested for malaria, even if they followed the doctor's advice.

source: Kemenkes 3M Plus campaign (via Dinas Kesehatan Provinsi Kepulauan Riau)
title: 3M Plus: drain, cover and recycle water containers
text: Indonesia's 3M Plus campaign targets the dengue mosquito Aedes aegypti, which breeds in clean water inside containers. Menguras: drain and scrub water containers such as the bak mandi (bath tub) and buckets every week. Menutup: cover water storage tightly. Mendaur ulang: recycle or dispose of items that collect rainwater, such as used tyres, cans and bottles. Plus: use nets, screens and repellent to avoid bites.

title: Malaria and dengue mosquitoes need different protection
text: Malaria mosquitoes (Anopheles) bite from dusk to dawn and breed in ground water such as pools, swamps, rice fields and lagoons; the key tools are a net at night and a prompt test for fever. Dengue mosquitoes (Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus) bite in the daytime, especially in the morning and late afternoon, and breed in containers around homes; the key tools are removing water containers and daytime repellent. Nets matter less for dengue because Aedes bite in the day, and container clean-ups matter less for malaria because Anopheles rarely breed in containers.

source: Nature Communications (2025); Kemenkes figures reported by Kompas
title: Where malaria remains in Indonesia
text: Indonesia recorded roughly half a million malaria cases in 2024, and about 93% came from Tanah Papua, home to about 2% of the population. Lowland districts such as Keerom, Jayapura, Mimika and Sarmi carry the heaviest burden. East Nusa Tenggara (including Sumba) and parts of Maluku and Kalimantan still have transmission, while about 80% of districts are malaria-free. Many cases are never found, so testing anyone with a fever in these areas matters.

source: HumBug (Sinka et al. 2021; Li et al. 2017); Stanford Abuzz (Mukundarajan et al. 2017)
title: What a buzz detector can and cannot tell you
text: Phone microphones can pick up mosquito wingbeats, and research tools such as HumBug and Abuzz use them to detect mosquitoes and guess the species. Identifying Anopheles by sound is less accurate than identifying other species. A buzz detector measures whether a mosquito is present, not whether anyone has been infected, and it has not been shown to reduce malaria cases. Its result should lead to action: use a net tonight, remove standing water, and get tested if anyone has a fever.
